To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
2-O-hydroxy fatty acid derivatives are able to induce a transient opening of the blood–brain barrier, allowing the transfer of large proteins into the brain of living rodents.
near-infrared time-domain optical imaging enables the visualization of globulin transfer to the brain of living mice and rats after 2-O-diglycerol-mediated blood–brain barrier permeabilization.

2-O-hydroxyhexadecanoic acid, an endogenous metabolite of hexyldiglycerols, induces blood–brain barrier disruption and facilitates the transport of fluorescent-labeled globulines into the healthy brain of small animals.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the application of near-infrared time-domain optical imaging in the visualization of the distribution of fluorescently labeled globulins in small animal brains after blood–brain opening.
the development of new strategies to visualize proteins and antibodies in the brain in vivo.
the development and application of novel methods for the visualization of proteins in the brain.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
2-O-hyexyldiglyerol is able to open the blood-brain barrier and allow the entry of large molecules such as antibodies and that this opening can be visualized in vivo.

2-O-hydroxyhexadecylglyceryl ether is an efficient tool for opening the blood–brain barrier, and that the use of near-infrared fluorescence imaging is a valuable tool to monitor the transfer of macromolecules into the brain.
the use of the 2-O-hydroxyhexadecylglycerol (C16:1) as a blood–brain barrier (BBB) opening compound is not suitable for the development of a brain delivery system.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
2-O-hydroxyhexadecanoic acid, a component of 2-O-hydroyhexadecanoate (2-O-hexadecanoin), is the key molecule that opens the blood–brain barrier.

2-O-hediglycerol-mediated blood–brain barrier disruption allows the visualization of the biodistribution and fate of fluorescent proteins in the brain of small animals using near-infrared fluorescence time-domain imaging.
2-O-hed can be used as a blood-brain barrier opening agent to deliver antibodies into the brain.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the brain is accessible to antibodies and that the use of in vivo imaging can be used to monitor protein transfer into the brain.
the 2-O-hydroxydiglycerol-induced blood-brain barrier opening is a promising approach for the delivery of antibodies into the brain of living animals.
in vivo time-domain fluorescence measurements are a promising approach for the monitoring of proteins after blood–brain opening.
